summary: Say what you mean clearly, simply and in an order people can follow.
goals: Describe communication as a loop between sender and receiver
Structure any message using PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point
Adapt your words, tone and channel to your audience
idea: Communication is not what you say; it is what the other person understands. Every message travels from a sender, through a channel, to a receiver, and noise (distractions, assumptions, emotions) can distort it at every stage. The sender is responsible for checking that the meaning arrived.

Clear communicators lead with their main point, keep sentences short and support claims with a reason and an example. Whether you are asking a teacher for an extension or pitching an idea to your team, a clear structure makes you easier to say yes to.
oneLine: Good communication is measured by what the listener understood, not by what the speaker said.
steps: Point: state your main message in one sentence first, 'I would like an extension on my essay.'
Reason: give one clear reason, 'I was ill for three days and missed two lessons.'
Example: add a specific detail, 'I have a doctor's note and I have already finished the plan and first paragraph.'
Point: repeat the request, 'So could I please submit on Friday instead of Wednesday?'
scenarioSetup: Ibrahim needs help on a group project. In the group chat he writes a long message with a joke, a complaint about another member, a vague hint and no clear request.
scenarioWrong: Nobody replies for a day. Each person thinks someone else will answer, and the work stalls.
scenarioBetter: Point: 'Can someone take the slides for Thursday?'
Reason: 'I am finishing the research and will be late'
Example: 'The slides only need the three headings we agreed, about 30 minutes of work'
Point: 'Please reply with a thumbs-up if you can take them.'
mistakes: Mistake: burying the main point in the middle. Fix: Lead with the point.
Mistake: using jargon or long sentences. Fix: Choose short, plain words.
Mistake: never checking understanding. Fix: Ask, 'Does that make sense? What questions do you have?'
lab: (5 min) Take a long, messy message and underline the real point
(10 min) Rewrite three messages (an email, a text and a spoken request) using PREP
(10 min) In pairs, deliver one PREP message aloud; the listener repeats back what they understood
(5 min) Compare: was the meaning the same?
reflect: When was I misunderstood recently, and what could I have said differently?
Do I adjust how I talk to teachers, friends and elders, and why?
Which of my messages are too long?
takeaways: Meaning is what the receiver understands
Lead with your point
Check understanding instead of assuming it
challenge: This week, use PREP for three real messages (one spoken, one written, one request to an adult). Note the responses you got, and add the best example to your portfolio.

check.q: In the PREP method, what comes first?
Why does 'noise' matter in communication?
o: It can distort the message between sender and receiver

check.q: Who is responsible for checking that a message was understood?

summary: Learn to listen fully so that people feel heard and you actually understand them.
goals: Show the difference between hearing, listening and waiting to speak
Practise RASA: Receive, Appreciate, Summarise, Ask
Use paraphrasing to check you have understood
idea: Hearing is a sense; listening is a skill. Most of us listen at the speed of thought, which is much faster than speech, so our minds wander, plan replies or judge. Active listening means giving full attention, showing it and checking you understood.

Being listened to is rare, so it is powerful. A friend who listens well gets trusted with more, a teacher who listens learns what students really need, and a leader who listens avoids expensive mistakes. Listening is the cheapest way to win respect.
oneLine: Listen to understand, not to reply.
steps: Receive: put your phone away, face the speaker, make comfortable eye contact and do not interrupt
Appreciate: use small signals such as nodding and 'mm-hm' so the speaker knows you are following
Summarise: say it back in your own words, 'So you are saying...'
Ask: pose an open question that digs deeper, 'What was the hardest part for you?'
scenarioSetup: Kemi tries to tell her older brother Tunde that she is worried about her exams. Tunde is scrolling on his phone and replies, 'Yeah, yeah, you will be fine,' without looking up.
scenarioWrong: Kemi stops talking and feels that her worries are silly. Tunde never learns that she needs help with revision.
scenarioBetter: Receive: Tunde puts the phone face down and turns to her
Appreciate: nods as she speaks
Summarise: 'You are worried because you feel behind in Chemistry?'
Ask: 'What would help most: a revision plan, or someone to quiz you?'
mistakes: Mistake: interrupting to share your own story. Fix: Wait until they finish, then ask a question.
Mistake: planning your reply while they speak. Fix: Focus on their words and emotion.
Mistake: multitasking. Fix: Give 100 per cent attention, even if only for five minutes.
lab: (5 min) Listening test: a partner speaks for one minute while you do nothing but listen, then repeat the key points
(10 min) Practise RASA in trios: speaker, listener, observer who checks each step
(5 min) Rotate roles
(5 min) Discuss which signals made you feel most heard
reflect: Who listens to me best and what do they do?
What makes me stop listening: boredom, disagreement, my phone?
Whom do I need to listen to more carefully this week?
takeaways: Listening is active, not passive
Summarising proves you understood
Questions show you care
challenge: Have two conversations this week where you use RASA fully, with your phone away. Afterwards, note what the speaker revealed that you would otherwise have missed. Add a short reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: What does 'summarise' in RASA mean?
o: Repeat the speaker's main points in your own words

check.q: Which is an open question?
o: What was the hardest part for you?

check.q: A friend is telling you a worry while you check your phone. What is the problem?
o: Your lack of full attention tells them they do not matter

summary: Prepare, structure and deliver short talks confidently, and manage your nerves.
goals: Plan a 2-minute talk with an opening, three points and a close
Use voice, pace and pause to keep an audience with you
Manage speaking nerves with preparation and breathing
idea: Public speaking ranks among the most common fears, yet it is a skill that improves quickly with deliberate practice. Nerves are normal: they are your body preparing for something important. Great speakers do not remove nerves; they channel them into energy and prepare so well that the nerves have less to attack.

A good talk is simple. It has a hook that wins attention, a clear message, no more than three main points and a strong ending. Audiences forget details but remember how clear, honest and alive you were.
oneLine: Prepare, structure, practise out loud and let your nerves become energy.
steps: Open: start with a hook such as a surprising fact, a question or a short story, then say your main message
Three points: give three points maximum, each with one example or a story
Close: summarise the three points and end with a call to action or a memorable line
Practise: rehearse out loud at least three times, standing up, and time yourself
scenarioSetup: Chidi has to present his science project to the class. He writes a long script, reads from his paper, speaks very fast and ends with 'That is all, thank you.'
scenarioWrong: His classmates lose focus after 30 seconds. He forgets the key finding and feels it was a disaster.
scenarioBetter: Open: 'Did you know that a plastic bottle can last 450 years? My project shows a way to reuse it in three steps.'
Three points: collect, clean, reuse, each with a quick example
Close: 'Next time you finish a bottle, ask: collect, clean, reuse?'
Practise: rehearse three times, using notes with only keywords, and pause after each point.
mistakes: Mistake: reading every word. Fix: Use keyword notes and look up.
Mistake: speaking too fast. Fix: Pause at the end of each sentence and breathe.
Mistake: apologising ('Sorry, I am not good at this'). Fix: Begin with confidence; the audience is on your side.
lab: (5 min) Pick a topic you know and choose a hook
(10 min) Build a three-point outline on one page
(10 min) Deliver a 2-minute talk to a partner; they time you and note one strength and one improvement
(5 min) Do a second round using the feedback
reflect: What happens in my body when I speak, and what helps?
Which speaker do I admire, and what do they do well?
What topic could I talk about with real energy?
takeaways: Nerves are normal and manageable
Structure keeps you and the audience on track
Practice out loud beats silent revision
challenge: Deliver a two-minute talk on a topic you care about to at least two different audiences (for example family and friends). Record or note feedback each time and add your outline and reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: How many main points are best for a short talk?
What is the best way to deal with speaking nerves?
o: Prepare well, practise out loud and breathe slowly

check.q: Why use keyword notes instead of a full script?
o: Notes let you look up and sound natural
It is easier to forget words

summary: Use story structure to make your message memorable and persuasive.
goals: Explain why stories are remembered better than facts alone
Build a personal story using Situation, Struggle, Solution, Lesson
Tell a 90-second story that connects to your audience
idea: Humans have shared stories for tens of thousands of years, and our brains are wired to remember them. A story places facts in a sequence with a character, a problem and a change, which gives the listener something to feel and picture. That is why people often forget the slides but remember the story.

Good stories are not long or fancy. A true, specific moment, such as the day you failed a test or helped a stranger, can teach more than a lecture. Stories build trust because they show who you are, not just what you know.
oneLine: Facts tell, stories stick: give your message a character, a struggle and a change.
methodName: The Story Spine: Situation, Struggle, Solution, Lesson
steps: Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences, who, where, when
Struggle: describe the problem or challenge honestly, including how you felt
Solution: explain what you did or what changed, with specific details
Lesson: finish with what you learned and why it matters to your listener
scenarioSetup: Hassana must introduce herself at a leadership camp. She says: 'My name is Hassana, I am 14, I like reading and I want to be a leader.' Nobody remembers it.
scenarioWrong: She lists facts without a story, so nothing sticks and she blends into the crowd.
scenarioBetter: Situation: 'Last year I was too shy to speak in class.'
Struggle: 'When my teacher asked me to read aloud, my voice shook and I wanted to disappear.'
Solution: 'I joined the school radio club and read the news every Friday for a term.'
Lesson: 'Now I know that courage is a muscle: I want to help other shy students find their voice.'
mistakes: Mistake: starting with a long background. Fix: Start close to the action.
Mistake: leaving out the struggle. Fix: A story needs a problem to matter.
Mistake: ending without a lesson. Fix: Link the story to your listener's life.
lab: (5 min) List three moments from your life that changed you
(10 min) Choose one and draft it using the Story Spine
(10 min) Tell it to a partner in 90 seconds; they note the most vivid detail
(5 min) Trim anything that does not support the lesson
reflect: Which story from my life shows who I really am?
What detail would make my story more vivid?
Whom could I tell my story to this week, and what would I want them to take away?
takeaways: Stories are easier to remember than facts
Honesty about the struggle builds trust
End with a lesson that connects to the listener
challenge: Write and tell a 90-second personal story using the Story Spine to at least two people, and note their reactions. Add the written version to your portfolio; it may become part of your personal statement later in the year.

check.q: What does a good story need in order to matter?
Why do stories help people remember messages?
o: They link facts to emotions and images

check.q: In the Story Spine, what does 'Lesson' do?
o: Connects the story to why it matters to the listener

summary: Understand how posture, face, eyes and voice send messages before you say a word.
goals: Describe the four channels of body language: posture, face, eyes and voice
Match your body language to your words so people trust you
Read others' signals carefully without jumping to conclusions
idea: People form impressions in seconds, and much of it comes from non-verbal signals: how you stand, whether you smile, where you look, how you sound. When your words and your body language disagree, people usually believe the body. Saying 'I am happy to help' with crossed arms and a frown does not feel believable.

Body language is also not a secret code. A single signal can mean many things: crossed arms may mean cold, not hostile. The skill is to notice clusters of signals, stay curious and, when in doubt, ask. It is also something you can adjust, such as standing tall or pausing, to feel and look more confident.
oneLine: Align your words with your posture, face, eyes and voice, and read others with curiosity, not certainty.
methodName: The Four Channels: Posture, Face, Eyes, Voice
steps: Posture: stand or sit tall with open shoulders; avoid hiding behind arms or a bag
Face: let your expression match your message; a natural smile at the start helps
Eyes: share eye contact in short, comfortable bursts; look at people one by one when presenting
Voice: vary volume, pace and tone; slow down and pause on key points
scenarioSetup: Obinna goes into an interview for a youth leadership programme. He mumbles, looks at the floor, slouches and says, 'I am very passionate.'
scenarioWrong: The panel sees nervousness and hears low energy, so they doubt his claim.
scenarioBetter: Posture: sit upright with feet flat and hands relaxed
Face: smile when greeting and show interest while listening
Eyes: make eye contact with whoever asks the question, then glance to others
Voice: speak a little slower and clearer, and pause before answering
mistakes: Mistake: copying a 'power pose' without meaning it. Fix: Aim to look natural, not forced.
Mistake: assuming one gesture proves what someone feels. Fix: Look for clusters and check by asking.
Mistake: staring without breaks. Fix: Use soft eye contact for a few seconds at a time.
lab: (5 min) Say 'I am really happy to be here' with three different body languages and ask a partner what they believed
(10 min) Watch a short clip with the sound off and describe what you think is happening
(10 min) Practise a one-minute introduction using the Four Channels
(5 min) Give each other one comment on a strength and one adjustment
reflect: What does my body do when I am nervous?
Which signals do I notice most in others?
Whose body language makes me feel at ease and why?
takeaways: Body language often outweighs words
Match your signals to your message
Read others with curiosity and ask when unsure
challenge: Practise the Four Channels in three real situations this week (for example greeting, answering a question, thanking someone). Ask a trusted person for feedback and note one thing to keep and one to change. Add your notes to your portfolio.

check.q: What do people usually believe when words and body language disagree?
Why should you be careful when reading body language?
o: One signal can have many meanings, so look for clusters and ask
It is always the same in every culture

check.q: Which set of signals best supports a message of confidence?
o: Open posture, steady voice and comfortable eye contact

summary: Work well in a team: share roles, agree rules and handle the stages of group work.
goals: Describe the four stages teams go through: forming, storming, norming, performing
Agree a team charter with roles, rules and a way to decide
Give and receive feedback that helps the team
idea: Almost every important task today, from a school project to a company launch, is done in teams. A good team is more than a group of friendly people: it has clear roles, shared goals and agreed ways of working. Psychologist Bruce Tuckman described stages most teams pass through: forming (getting to know each other), storming (friction), norming (agreeing how to work) and performing (doing great work).

Disagreement in the storming stage is normal and does not mean the team has failed. Teams that talk early about roles, communication and deadlines move through it faster. A short team charter written at the start prevents most of the arguments that wreck group projects.
oneLine: Great teams agree on roles, rules and goals early, and treat disagreement as part of the process.
steps: Goal: write one sentence saying what success looks like, and the deadline
Roles: assign clear jobs such as lead, researcher, designer, presenter and time-keeper; everyone has one
Rules: agree how you will communicate (group chat, meeting days), how you decide (discuss, then vote) and what happens if someone misses a deadline
Check-in: schedule a short review at the halfway point to adjust roles and share feedback
scenarioSetup: A group of four students has two weeks to build a model of a water filter. Two members do all the work, one keeps joking and one never replies to messages.
scenarioWrong: With no charter, resentment grows. The hard workers complain to the teacher and the project is submitted late and incomplete.
scenarioBetter: Goal: 'A working filter and a three-minute demo by Friday the 14th'
Roles: designer, builder, tester, presenter
Rules: reply to messages within 24 hours; meet Tuesday and Thursday for 30 minutes; if someone is stuck, ask early
Check-in: on day seven, review who needs help and swap tasks if needed
mistakes: Mistake: letting one person do everything. Fix: Give each person a role and a visible task.
Mistake: avoiding conflict until it explodes. Fix: Raise issues early, using calm 'I' statements.
Mistake: judging members by personality instead of contribution. Fix: Discuss behaviour and outcomes, not character.
lab: (5 min) In groups of four, choose a mini-project, such as planning a class event
(10 min) Write a team charter: goal, roles, rules, check-in
(10 min) Run a mock 'storming' moment: one member misses a deadline; practise resolving it respectfully
(5 min) Share one lesson with the class
reflect: What role do I naturally take in groups, and what role would stretch me?
What was my best team experience, and what made it work?
What do I do when I disagree with a teammate?
takeaways: Teams work best with shared goals and clear roles
Storming is normal and solvable
A charter prevents most conflict
challenge: Use a team charter in a real group task this week (school, church, sport or family). Record what worked and what you would change. Add your charter and reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: Which stage of Tuckman's model usually involves friction between members?
What is the main purpose of a team charter?
o: To agree goals, roles and rules early

check.q: Two members do all the work while others coast. What would have helped most?

summary: Handle disagreements calmly, express your needs clearly and find solutions that work for both sides.
goals: Describe conflict as a normal difference in needs, not a fight to win
Use 'I' statements: Observe, Feel, Need, Request
Aim for a solution that meets both sides' key needs
idea: Conflict happens whenever people with different needs, values or goals share a space. It is not the same as fighting. Handled badly, conflict damages friendships; handled well, it clarifies expectations and can strengthen relationships.

Most conflicts escalate because we attack the person ('You are lazy') instead of describing the problem ('The dishes were left yesterday'). Psychologist Marshall Rosenberg's approach, called nonviolent communication, uses four steps: observe, feel, need, request. It keeps the conversation about needs and solutions rather than blame.
oneLine: Describe the behaviour, own your feeling, state your need and make a clear request.
steps: Observe: describe what happened without judgement, 'You were 30 minutes late to our meeting'
Feel: say how you felt, 'I felt frustrated and unimportant'
Need: say what you need, 'I need reliable timing so our work gets done'
Request: ask for a specific action, 'Could you text me if you will be late?' and listen to their side
scenarioSetup: Nneka and her cousin share a bedroom. Nneka has an exam tomorrow, but her cousin keeps playing loud music.
scenarioWrong: Nneka shouts, 'You are so selfish!' Her cousin shouts back and they do not speak for two days.
scenarioBetter: Observe: 'The music has been loud for an hour.'
Feel: 'I feel stressed because I am worried about my exam.'
Need: 'I need quiet to study until 9 pm.'
Request: 'Could you use headphones until 9, and I will leave you alone for the rest of the evening?'
mistakes: Mistake: using 'always' and 'never'. Fix: Describe the specific event.
Mistake: bringing up old issues. Fix: Stick to the one problem.
Mistake: winning the argument. Fix: Aim for a solution both can live with.
lab: (5 min) Read three conflict scenarios and rewrite blaming sentences into 'I' statements
(10 min) Role-play a real-life conflict in pairs using Observe, Feel, Need, Request
(5 min) Swap roles
(5 min) Discuss how it felt to hear an 'I' statement compared with an attack
reflect: How do I usually react in conflict: fight, flee, freeze or fix?
Which conflict from the past needs repair?
What need was hidden behind my last argument?
takeaways: Conflict is normal; harm is optional
Observe, Feel, Need, Request keeps talks calm
Look for solutions where both sides get what matters
challenge: Use Observe, Feel, Need, Request in one real disagreement this week (or rehearse it in writing if no conflict arises). Write what happened and what you would adjust next time, and add it to your portfolio.

check.q: Which sentence is an 'I' statement?
o: I felt ignored when my idea was skipped, and I need to be heard

check.q: What is the aim of a win-win approach?
o: To find a solution that meets both sides' key needs

check.q: Why avoid words like 'always' and 'never' in conflicts?
o: They exaggerate and make the other person defensive

summary: Negotiate by focusing on interests, preparing options and finding trades that both sides can accept.
goals: Tell the difference between positions and interests
Prepare for a negotiation with a goal, a walk-away point and options
Use Ask, Offer, Trade to reach a fair agreement
idea: Negotiation is not only for business deals. You negotiate whenever you ask for a later deadline, agree who does which chore or decide where to eat. The aim is a fair agreement that both sides will keep, not to defeat the other person.

The classic mistake is arguing about positions (what each person says they want) instead of interests (why they want it). Two sisters fighting over the last orange may discover that one wants the juice and the other wants the peel for a cake: both can win. Preparation matters too: know what you want, what you can give and what you will do if there is no deal.
oneLine: Look behind positions to interests, prepare your options, then trade so both sides gain.
steps: Prepare: write your goal, your minimum acceptable outcome and your best alternative if there is no deal
Ask: start by asking questions to understand their interests, 'What is most important to you here?'
Offer: share your interests and propose options; give a reason, not just a demand
Trade: swap things that cost you little but matter to them, such as 'If you help with the poster, I will present'; then confirm the agreement
scenarioSetup: Musa wants his parents to extend his weekend curfew from 8 pm to 10 pm. They say no, because they worry about safety. Musa sulks and slams the door.
scenarioWrong: He argues only about the time. His parents dig in, and he loses the chance to discuss the real concern.
scenarioBetter: Prepare: goal 10 pm; minimum 9 pm; plan B is a trial for one month
Ask: 'What worries you most about me being out late?' They say transport and knowing where he is
Offer: 'I will share my location, travel with two friends and text when I arrive.'
Trade: 'Can we try 9:30 pm for one month, then review?' They agree.
mistakes: Mistake: opening with an extreme demand. Fix: Be ambitious but reasonable.
Mistake: treating it as a fight. Fix: Remember you must live with the person afterwards.
Mistake: accepting the first offer. Fix: Ask for a moment to think and explore trades.
lab: (5 min) Read a scenario with two positions and list each person's possible interests
(10 min) In pairs, negotiate a classroom or home rule using Prepare, Ask, Offer, Trade
(5 min) Swap sides and replay
(5 min) Debrief: what trades surprised you?
reflect: What do I usually negotiate for: time, money, attention, freedom?
Do I give in too fast or push too hard?
Which relationship needs a fairer agreement?
takeaways: Interests matter more than positions
Preparation changes outcomes
The best deals create value for both sides
challenge: Plan and conduct one real negotiation this week (for example chores, screen time, a deadline). Write your preparation, the outcome and what you would change. Add it to your portfolio.

check.q: What is an 'interest' in negotiation?
o: The underlying reason someone wants something

check.q: Why prepare a minimum acceptable outcome?
o: So you know when to say yes or walk away
So you can ask for nothing

check.q: Two sisters want the same orange. One needs the juice, the other the peel. What best solves it?
o: Cut it in half by weight
Discover interests and give each what they need

summary: Lead by serving: see a need, act with humility and measure whether people were really helped.
goals: Explain servant leadership and how it differs from leading by power
Use See, Serve, Reflect to lead a small act of service
Identify a need in your school or community that you could address
idea: Leadership is not a title; it is influence used for good. Servant leadership, a term coined by Robert Greenleaf, flips the usual picture: the leader's first job is to serve the people they lead, by listening, removing obstacles and helping others grow. The test is whether those served become healthier, wiser and more capable.

You do not need a position to lead through service. Cleaning a shared space, mentoring a younger student or organising a food drive are all leadership. Serving also builds skills you need later: planning, empathy, persuasion and humility.
oneLine: Lead by serving: notice a need, act with humility and check that people truly benefited.
steps: See: look and listen for a real need, and ask the people affected what they need, rather than guessing
Serve: choose a small, doable action, recruit helpers and do the work without needing credit
Reflect: ask the people served and your team, 'Did this help? What would make it better?'
Repeat: improve the idea and invite others to lead the next round
scenarioSetup: Ejike notices that junior students at his school eat lunch alone on the first week of term because they do not know anyone.
scenarioWrong: He posts a speech on social media about 'bullying' but takes no action. Nothing changes for the juniors.
scenarioBetter: See: he talks to three juniors, who say they feel nervous and lost
Serve: with two friends he starts a 'Lunch Buddies' table and invites juniors to join games
Reflect: after two weeks, they ask the juniors for feedback and learn that a short orientation tour also helps
Repeat: they add the tour, and a Year 9 team takes over next term.
mistakes: Mistake: serving for applause. Fix: Focus on the impact, not the photo.
Mistake: deciding what people need without asking. Fix: Listen first.
Mistake: starting too big and burning out. Fix: Begin with a small, repeatable action.
lab: (5 min) List three needs you see at school, at home and in your community
(10 min) Choose one and map the See, Serve, Reflect steps
(10 min) Plan a mini-project: who, what, when, how you will measure success
(5 min) Pitch it to a partner in 60 seconds
reflect: When has someone served me without expecting anything back?
Who is overlooked in my school or neighbourhood?
What does 'success' look like for a service project?
takeaways: Leadership is influence used to help others
Ask people what they need before acting
Measure impact by whether lives improve
challenge: Complete one act of service you planned in the lab, with at least one other person involved. Collect feedback from those served and record the impact. Add your plan, evidence and reflection to your Community Service record.

check.q: What is the first job of a servant leader?
o: To serve the people they lead

check.q: Why ask people what they need before serving?
o: To avoid guessing and actually address real needs

check.q: What is the best measure of a service project's success?

summary: Build genuine professional relationships by introducing yourself well, asking good questions and following up.
goals: Explain networking as building relationships, not collecting contacts
Prepare a 30-second introduction and two good questions
Follow up within 48 hours and keep the relationship alive
idea: Networking simply means building a circle of people who know you, trust you and want to help you, and whom you also want to help. Most opportunities, such as internships, scholarships and advice, come through people. The best networkers are curious, generous and consistent, not pushy.

A good first meeting is short and genuine. You introduce yourself clearly, show interest in the other person and ask a question that invites a story. The real work happens afterwards: a thank-you message, a useful link or an update keeps the relationship alive.
oneLine: Networking is about being curious, helpful and consistent, and following up.
steps: Prepare: know who will be there and write a 30-second introduction (name, what you do or study, what you are curious about)
Introduce: smile, give a firm greeting, say your introduction and ask their name and role
Ask: use open questions, 'How did you get into this work?' and 'What advice would you give someone my age?'
Follow up: within 48 hours send a short message, 'Thank you for speaking with me. I enjoyed hearing about...'; offer something in return when you can
scenarioSetup: At a school career fair, Ope stands near the wall and speaks only when a speaker asks her a question. She leaves without any names.
scenarioWrong: Weeks later she wants advice about engineering but knows no one to ask.
scenarioBetter: Prepare: 'Hi, I am Ope, a Year 10 student who loves building things. I am curious about engineering.'
Introduce: she greets the civil engineer, says her line and asks for her name
Ask: 'What did you enjoy most about your degree?'
Follow up: she sends a thank-you message on LinkedIn or email, and later shares a photo of her school project.
mistakes: Mistake: asking for a favour immediately. Fix: Build rapport first.
Mistake: only talking about yourself. Fix: Aim for 70 per cent listening.
Mistake: never following up. Fix: Set a reminder for 48 hours.
lab: (5 min) Write your 30-second introduction
(10 min) Practise a mini networking event: move around and talk to three people using your introduction and two questions
(5 min) Draft a follow-up message
(5 min) Share one thing you learned about a classmate
reflect: What stops me from starting conversations with new people?
Who could I help with something I know?
Who should I follow up with this week?
takeaways: Networking is relationships, not collecting contacts
Good questions beat clever introductions
Follow-up turns a meeting into a connection
challenge: Meet or message two new people in an area you are curious about. Use your introduction and questions, send a follow-up within 48 hours and record what you learned. Add your notes to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the best aim of networking?
o: Collecting as many contacts as possible
Making people remember your name by force

check.q: When should you send a follow-up message?
Which question works best to start a conversation?
o: Can you give me a job?
How did you get into this work?

summary: Work effectively with people from different cultures by staying curious, learning and adapting.
goals: Explain what cultural intelligence (CQ) is and why it matters
Describe the iceberg model of culture: visible behaviour and hidden values
Use the CQ cycle: Drive, Knowledge, Strategy, Action
idea: Culture is the shared habits, beliefs and values of a group. It shapes how people greet each other, how they treat time, how direct they are and how they show respect. Cultural intelligence (CQ) is the ability to work well across cultures by being curious, learning and adjusting your behaviour.

A helpful picture is an iceberg: above the water you see food, clothes, language and festivals; below the water sit values, beliefs and assumptions that drive them. When behaviour surprises you, ask what hidden value might be behind it. Culture also includes differences within a country, such as between regions, religions and generations.
oneLine: Be curious, learn what is beneath the surface, plan how to adapt and act with respect.
methodName: The CQ Cycle: Drive, Knowledge, Strategy, Action
steps: Drive: show real interest and confidence in learning about people from other backgrounds
Knowledge: learn about their customs, values and communication styles from reliable sources and the people themselves
Strategy: before meeting, plan how you will adjust, for example how formal to be and how to greet
Action: adapt your behaviour respectfully, ask when unsure and reflect afterwards on what you learned
scenarioSetup: A Nigerian student joins an online project team with students from Japan, Germany and Brazil. In the first call, the Japanese student rarely speaks, the German student is very direct and the Brazilian student arrives 10 minutes late and apologises warmly.
scenarioWrong: The Nigerian student concludes, 'The Japanese student is not interested, the German is rude and the Brazilian is lazy,' and gives them a low rating.
scenarioBetter: Drive: she decides to understand rather than judge
Knowledge: she learns that in some cultures people wait to be invited to speak, directness is seen as honesty and time norms vary
Strategy: she plans to invite quieter members by name and agree a start time
Action: 'Kenji, would you like to share your view?' and 'Let us agree meetings start at 5:00 with a five-minute buffer.'
mistakes: Mistake: stereotyping a whole nation from one person. Fix: Treat each person as an individual first.
Mistake: judging others by your own norms. Fix: Ask what the behaviour means to them.
Mistake: staying silent for fear of offending. Fix: Ask respectfully; people appreciate genuine curiosity.
lab: (5 min) Draw an iceberg for your own culture: three visible things and three hidden values
(10 min) In groups, read a cross-cultural misunderstanding case and identify the hidden values
(10 min) Plan how you would behave using the CQ cycle
(5 min) Share one insight
reflect: What do I assume is 'normal' that may not be normal elsewhere?
When did I feel excluded or misunderstood because of culture?
Which culture would I like to learn about, and how?
takeaways: Visible behaviour rests on hidden values
Curiosity beats assumption
Adapting is a sign of respect, not weakness
challenge: Have a conversation with someone from a different cultural, regional or generational background and ask what values matter most to them. Write what surprised you and how you would adapt. Add your reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: In the iceberg model, what is below the surface?
What should you do when someone's behaviour surprises you?
o: Ask what it means to them and stay curious

check.q: Why is stereotyping a risk?
o: It treats individuals as if they are all the same
